# Organizing your project {#project}

::: {.goals}
**In this chapter**

- how to lay out a project directory with `data`, `scripts`, `results`,
  `figs`, and `manuscript` folders
- how to document where your data came from in a `data/README.md`
- how to make an RStudio project
- how to keep a project notebook in R Markdown that records everything you
  did: the commands, the software versions, and the results
- how to write Markdown
:::

## Why organize? {#why-organize}

The most important collaborator on any project is you, six months from now.
By then you'll have forgotten which file is the raw data, which script made
Figure 3, and what options you gave the aligner. A reviewer will ask, or a
labmate will want to build on your work, or you'll find a bug and need to
redo everything downstream of it.

Organizing a project well isn't hard, and you only have to decide how once. The
layout in this chapter follows two widely read papers that are worth a few
minutes of your time:

- Noble (2009). [A quick guide to organizing computational biology
  projects](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1000424). *PLoS
  Computational Biology* 5: e1000424.
- Wilson et al. (2017). [Good enough practices in scientific
  computing](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005510). *PLoS
  Computational Biology* 13: e1005510.

The guiding principle, from Noble: someone unfamiliar with your project
should be able to look at your files and understand exactly what you did and
why.

## A directory for each project {#project-layout}

Put each project in its own directory, with the same set of folders every
time:

| Folder        | What goes in it                                                     |
|---------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `data/`       | raw data, exactly as you received or downloaded it, plus a `README.md` saying where it came from |
| `scripts/`    | your code: shell scripts, Python, R                                 |
| `results/`    | intermediate files made by your scripts: filtered and processed data, tables, alignments, trees, program output |
| `figs/`       | figures, made by your scripts                                       |
| `manuscript/` | the paper, poster, or thesis chapter                                |

Data flow in one direction: scripts read raw data from `data/` and write what
they make to `results/`; later scripts read from `results/` and write more
results, or figures in `figs/`. Nothing a script makes ever goes in `data/`.

At the top level go a `README.md` describing the project and the project
**notebook** (Section \@ref(notebook)).

Inside these folders, add subdirectories wherever they help you, or someone
else, find things. Organize each folder by what's in it. Our example project,
on the genome of the diatom *Phaeodactylum tricornutum*, uses two kinds of
data: the published genome sequence and our own RNA-seq reads:

```text
phaeodactylum_project/
├── README.md
├── notebook.Rmd
├── phaeodactylum_project.Rproj
├── data/
│   ├── README.md
│   ├── genome/
│   └── rnaseq/
├── scripts/
│   └── seq_lengths.sh
├── results/
│   ├── 2026-01-16_seq_lengths/
│   ├── 2026-02-02_assembly_k21/
│   ├── 2026-02-03_assembly_k33/
│   └── 2026-02-05_assembly_k55/
├── figs/
└── manuscript/
```

- **`data/`** is divided by source: one subdirectory for each data set, each
  described in `data/README.md` (Section \@ref(data-readme)).
- **`results/`** is divided by analysis: each time you run an analysis, its
  output goes in a new subdirectory named with the date and what it is
  (Section \@ref(project-rules)).
- **`scripts/`** and **`figs/`** stay flat, with descriptive file names,
  until there are enough files that subdirectories would help.

::: {.note}
**Why not a `genome/` and `rnaseq/` folder everywhere?** You'll sometimes see
projects that repeat the same subdirectories inside `data`, `scripts`,
`results`, and `figs`. That can work, but it's rarely as clean as it looks: a
script often uses data from more than one part of the project, a figure
combines several results, and the parts of a project change as it goes.
Start simple, and add subdirectories when a folder gets crowded.
:::

### Making the directories {#mkdir-braces}

You could make these one at a time with `mkdir`, but the shell has a shortcut.
**Brace expansion** turns a comma-separated list in braces into several
words. See what it does with `echo`:

```{bash}
echo {data,scripts,results,figs,manuscript}
echo sample_{A,B,C}_{R1,R2}.fastq.gz
```

Two sets of braces give every combination. Braces can also go inside other
braces, so one `mkdir` makes the whole tree. `-p` makes the parent directory,
`phaeodactylum_project`, along the way (Section \@ref(managing-files)):

```{bash, sandbox = TRUE}
mkdir -p phaeodactylum_project/{data/{genome,rnaseq},scripts,results,figs,manuscript}
find phaeodactylum_project -type d | sort
```

::: {.warning}
**No spaces inside the braces.** `{data, scripts}` doesn't expand, because
the space splits it into two separate words. The same goes for spaces in file
and directory names generally (Section \@ref(file-system)).
:::

::: {.tip}
**Prefer pictures?** The `tree` command draws a directory tree like the one
above. It isn't installed by default: `brew install tree` on a Mac,
`sudo apt install tree` on Linux.
:::

### Rules of thumb {#project-rules}

- **One project, one directory.** Everything a project needs lives inside it,
  so you can move it, copy it to the cluster, or put it on GitHub as one unit.
- **Raw data are read-only.** Never edit raw data by hand. Scripts read the
  raw data and write their output to `results/`. To protect raw data from
  accidents, remove write permission (Section \@ref(chmod)):
  `chmod -R a-w data/genome`.
- **Everything in `results/` and `figs/` can be remade** by running your
  scripts. If you deleted either folder, you should be able to get it back.
  That's why the notebook records every command (Section \@ref(notebook)).
  Results can be big, so they're often left out of Git (Section
  \@ref(gitignore)) and backed up separately if they took a long time to make.
- **Organize results by analysis.** When you run the same analysis
  several ways, give each run its own subdirectory, such as
  `results/2026-02-03_assembly_k33/`, so new output never overwrites old
  output and the date links it to its notebook entry.
- **Use relative paths** inside the project, such as
  `results/2026-01-16_seq_lengths/seq_lengths.tsv`, not
  `/Users/aja/Desktop/phaeodactylum_project/results/2026-01-16_seq_lengths/seq_lengths.tsv`.
  Then the project works on any computer, in any location.
- **Name files so they sort.** Use dates in the form `2026-01-14` (year
  first), and number scripts that run in order: `01_download.sh`,
  `02_seq_lengths.sh`, `03_plot.R`. Use leading zeros (`01`, not `1`) so `10`
  sorts after `09`.
- **No spaces in names** (Section \@ref(file-system)).

### Marking the final result {#final-result}

Most analyses are run more than once: with a range of parameter settings,
on different subsets of the data, or again after you fix a bug. That's as it
should be, but months later, when a reviewer asks about Figure 2, which of
the dozen runs did you actually publish?

Don't copy the chosen output somewhere else, and don't rename it. Leave every
run where it is, and make a **symbolic link** (Section \@ref(ln)) called
`FINAL_PUBLISHED_RESULT` that points to the exact file you used. Suppose we
assembled a genome with three different *k*-mer sizes, and the paper uses the
assembly made with *k* = 33:

```{bash, sandbox = TRUE, dir = "phaeodactylum_project/results", echo = FALSE, results = "hide"}
for k in 21 33 55; do
  mkdir -p 2026-02-0${k:0:1}_assembly_k$k
  echo ">contig_1 k=$k" > 2026-02-0${k:0:1}_assembly_k$k/contigs.fasta
done
```

```{bash, sandbox = TRUE, dir = "phaeodactylum_project/results"}
ls
```

Go to the directory where the link should live, and make the link:

```{bash, sandbox = TRUE, dir = "phaeodactylum_project/results"}
ln -s 2026-02-03_assembly_k33/contigs.fasta FINAL_PUBLISHED_RESULT
ls -l
```

`ls -l` shows where the link points (`->`), and the `l` at the start of the
line marks it as a link. Anything that reads the link reads the real file:

```{bash, sandbox = TRUE, dir = "phaeodactylum_project/results"}
head -n 1 FINAL_PUBLISHED_RESULT
```

Now the answer is obvious to you, your coauthors, and anyone who reuses your
project, and the runs you didn't use are still there for comparison. A few
tips:

- **Its name is in capitals** so it stands out in a directory listing.
- **Make one link per published result.** If a paper uses several, give each
  link a descriptive suffix, such as `FINAL_PUBLISHED_RESULT_fig2` and
  `FINAL_PUBLISHED_RESULT_table1`. The same works for figures: put a
  `FINAL_PUBLISHED_FIG2` link in `figs/`.
- **Changed your mind?** `ln -sf` replaces an existing link:
  `ln -sf 2026-02-05_assembly_k55/contigs.fasta FINAL_PUBLISHED_RESULT`.
- **Record the choice in your notebook**, with the reason: "Used the *k* = 33
  assembly: highest N50 and BUSCO completeness of the three."

::: {.warning}
**A link's target is relative to the link, not to you.** `ln -s` stores the
path to the target exactly as you typed it, and the system follows it from
the directory where the link lives. If you're at the top of the project and
type `ln -s results/2026-02-03_assembly_k33/contigs.fasta
results/FINAL_PUBLISHED_RESULT`, the link looks for
`results/2026-02-03_assembly_k33/...` *inside* `results/`, and finds
nothing: a
**broken link**. That's why it's easiest to `cd` to the directory where the
link should live first. Check a new link with `head` or `ls -L`, which show
an error if the link is broken.
:::

::: {.tip}
**Keep links relative.** A link to a relative path, like the one above, keeps
working when you move or copy the whole project, because the files it points
to move with it. A link to an absolute path
(`/Users/aja/Desktop/phaeodactylum_project/...`) breaks as soon as the project
moves. `rsync -a` (Section \@ref(rsync)) copies links as links, and Git stores
them as links, too.
:::

## Documenting your data {#data-readme}

Every `data` directory gets its own `README.md` that says, for each data set:
what it is, where it came from (a URL or accession number), when and how you
got it, and its checksums (a kind of digital fingerprint for a file, covered
in Section \@ref(checksums)). This is the first thing
you'll need when you write the methods section, and the first thing anyone
reusing your data will look for.

Here's how the genome data in our example project were downloaded. NCBI
provides checksums for every file, so we check that the download is intact.
Don't worry about the details yet: downloading with `curl` and checking files
with `md5sum` are covered in Chapter \@ref(remote) (Sections \@ref(download)
and \@ref(checksums)). For now, notice what gets recorded:

```{bash, eval = FALSE}
cd data/genome
curl -O https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCF/000/150/955/GCF_000150955.2_ASM15095v2/GCF_000150955.2_ASM15095v2_genomic.fna.gz
curl -O https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCF/000/150/955/GCF_000150955.2_ASM15095v2/md5checksums.txt
md5sum GCF_000150955.2_ASM15095v2_genomic.fna.gz
grep ASM15095v2_genomic.fna.gz md5checksums.txt
```

```
9f3ceb6ed3a6c00bd1019a44fdcf4256  GCF_000150955.2_ASM15095v2_genomic.fna.gz
9f3ceb6ed3a6c00bd1019a44fdcf4256  ./GCF_000150955.2_ASM15095v2_genomic.fna.gz
```

Our checksum (first line) matches NCBI's (second line). And here's the `data/README.md`
that records it all. It's written in Markdown (Section \@ref(markdown)):

```markdown
# Data for the Phaeodactylum genome project

## genome/

Reference genome of *Phaeodactylum tricornutum* CCAP 1055/1, RefSeq assembly
GCF_000150955.2 (ASM15095v2), from NCBI:
<https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/datasets/genome/GCF_000150955.2/>

Downloaded 2026-01-14 by Your Name. Commands are in `notebook.Rmd`.

| File                                        | Contents                 | MD5                              |
|---------------------------------------------|--------------------------|----------------------------------|
| GCF_000150955.2_ASM15095v2_genomic.fna.gz   | genome sequence (FASTA)  | 9f3ceb6ed3a6c00bd1019a44fdcf4256 |
| md5checksums.txt                            | NCBI's checksums         |                                  |

## rnaseq/

RNA-seq reads, 6 samples, sequenced by the UAMS Genomics Core, received
2026-02-03 on a hard drive. Sample information is in `rnaseq/samples.csv`.
```

If one part of the project has a lot of data, it can have its own README, for
example `data/rnaseq/README.md`, with `data/README.md` pointing to it.

## RStudio projects {#rstudio-projects}

[RStudio](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/) is the most popular
program for working in R, and it's a good home base for a project even when
most of the work happens in the shell. An **RStudio project** is a project
directory with a small settings file, `phaeodactylum_project.Rproj`, at the
top level. Opening a project (double-click the `.Rproj` file, or use
*File > Open Project* in RStudio):

- sets R's working directory to the top of the project, so relative paths
  such as `results/2026-01-16_seq_lengths/seq_lengths.tsv` just work
- opens a *Terminal* tab (next to the *Console*) that also starts at the top
  of the project
- reopens the files you were working on, and keeps a separate history for
  each project

To turn the directory we made into an RStudio project:

1. In RStudio, choose *File > New Project...*
2. Choose **Existing Directory**, browse to `phaeodactylum_project`, and click
   **Create Project**.

RStudio restarts inside the project and creates `phaeodactylum_project.Rproj`
and a hidden `.Rproj.user/` directory of settings. (To start a project from
scratch instead, choose **New Directory** > **New Project**, then make the
folders from the Terminal tab.) The `.Rproj` file is short plain text:

```text
Version: 1.0

RestoreWorkspace: No
SaveWorkspace: No
AlwaysSaveHistory: Default

EnableCodeIndexing: Yes
Encoding: UTF-8
```

::: {.tip}
**Start each R session fresh.** In *Tools > Global Options > General*, uncheck
*Restore .RData into workspace at startup* and set *Save workspace to .RData
on exit* to **Never**. Otherwise R quietly carries old objects from one session
to the next, and code that works for you may fail for everyone else. If
everything important is made by scripts, you never need a saved workspace.
:::

## The project notebook {#notebook}

At the bench, you keep a lab notebook. A computational project needs one too.
The **project notebook** is where you document *everything* you do, as you do
it:

- what you did and why, dated
- the exact commands you ran, copied from the Terminal
- the **versions** of the software you used (results can change between
  versions, and the methods section needs them)
- the results, including the dead ends ("tried X; it didn't work because Y")
- what to do next

We'll keep the notebook in **R Markdown**, a plain-text format that mixes
Markdown text (Section \@ref(markdown)) with chunks of code. Knitting the file
turns it into a nicely formatted web page, with the code in shaded boxes.
(This book was written in R Markdown, too.)

### Making the notebook {#make-notebook}

In RStudio, with the project open:

1. Choose *File > New File > R Markdown...*
2. Give it a title, such as "Phaeodactylum genome project: notebook", and
   your name. Leave the output format as **HTML**. Click **OK**.
3. RStudio opens an example document. Delete everything below the header
   (the part between the two `---` lines), and save the file as
   `notebook.Rmd` at the top of the project.

Click **Knit** (or press <kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>K</kbd>) to turn
`notebook.Rmd` into `notebook.html`, and open it in a browser.

::: {.note}
**R Markdown or Quarto?** RStudio's *File > New File* menu also offers
**Quarto** documents (`.qmd`), the newer successor to R Markdown from the same
developers. They work almost the same way. This course uses R Markdown, which
is still fully supported.
:::

### What goes in the notebook {#notebook-contents}

Here's a notebook for our example project, a couple of days in. Entries are
in date order, each under a dated heading, with the commands in code chunks
and the results written out below them:

```{r notebook-template, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("````markdown", readLines("templates/notebook.Rmd"), "````", sep = "\n")
```

A few things to notice:

- **The header** (between the `---` lines) is written in YAML. It sets the
  title, author, and date, and `toc: true` adds a table of contents that
  floats beside the text (`toc_float`), so you can jump to any day.
- **Code chunks** start with ```` ```{bash} ```` or ```` ```{r} ```` and end
  with ```` ``` ````. RStudio shows them shaded, and the *Insert* menu (the
  green **+C** button above the editor) adds a new one.
- **`eval = FALSE`** in the setup chunk means knitting doesn't run the code.
  The notebook is a *record*: you ran the commands in the Terminal as you
  worked, and you don't want every knit to download the genome again. Turn a
  chunk back on with `eval = TRUE` in its header, as in the last chunk.
- **Software versions** are in a table, copied from each program's version
  command (`curl --version`, `samtools --version`, `blastn -version`). The
  last chunk runs `sessionInfo()`, which lists the versions of R and of every
  R package that was loaded.
- **Longer code goes in `scripts/`.** The notebook just records running it.
  Here's `scripts/seq_lengths.sh`, which uses `awk` (Section
  \@ref(awk)) to print the name and length of each sequence in a FASTA
  file:

```{bash, eval = FALSE}
#!/bin/bash
# Print the name and length of every sequence in the genome, tab-separated.
gzcat data/genome/GCF_000150955.2_ASM15095v2_genomic.fna.gz |
  awk '/^>/ {if (name) print name "\t" len; name = substr($1, 2); len = 0; next}
       {len += length($0)}
       END {print name "\t" len}'
```

::: {.tip}
**Write it down now.** The commands you think you'll remember are the ones
you'll forget. Paste each command into the notebook right after it works (or
right after it fails, with a note about why). `history` (Section
\@ref(history)) can help you recover what you typed.
:::

## Markdown {#markdown}

**Markdown** is a simple way to format plain text. You write `**bold**`, and
it becomes **bold**. It's everywhere in scientific computing: R Markdown and
Quarto documents, Jupyter notebooks, `README.md` files, and GitHub, which
displays Markdown files formatted. Because it's plain text, Markdown is easy to
read even before it's formatted, works with any text editor, and works well
with Git (Chapter \@ref(git)), which we'll use to keep track of every version
of your project.

### Text {-}

| You type                     | You get                     |
|------------------------------|-----------------------------|
| `*italic*` or `_italic_`     | *italic*                    |
| `**bold**`                   | **bold**                    |
| `` `code` ``                 | `code`                      |
| `~~strikethrough~~`          | ~~strikethrough~~           |
| `H~2~O`, `x^2^` (R Markdown) | H~2~O, x^2^                 |
| `[a link](https://www.uark.edu)` | [a link](https://www.uark.edu) |
| `<https://www.uark.edu>`     | <https://www.uark.edu>      |

Use italics for species names: `*Phaeodactylum tricornutum*`.

**Paragraphs** are separated by a blank line. A single line break inside a
paragraph is ignored, so you can break long lines wherever you like. To start
a new paragraph, leave a blank line.

### Headings {-}

Start a line with one to six `#` characters, followed by a space:

```markdown
# Heading 1
## Heading 2
### Heading 3
```

### Lists {-}

Start each item with `-` (or `*`) for a bulleted list, or a number and a
period for a numbered list. Indent by four spaces to nest a list inside
another. Leave a blank line before a list.

```markdown
Things to buy:

- agarose
- primers
    - ITS1
    - ITS4

Steps:

1. Extract DNA.
2. Amplify.
3. Sequence.
```

### Code {-}

Inline code goes between single backticks, `` `like this` ``. For a block of
code, put three backticks on the lines before and after. Add the language
after the opening backticks to color-code it:

````markdown
```bash
grep -c '>' sequences.fasta
```
````

In R Markdown, a language in *braces*, such as ```` ```{bash} ```` or
```` ```{r} ````, makes a code chunk that can be run, not just displayed.

### Images, tables, and quotes {-}

```markdown
![A caption for the figure](figs/seq_lengths.png)

| Sample | Reads     |
|--------|-----------|
| A1     | 1,204,551 |
| A2     |   998,013 |

> A block quote starts with a greater-than sign.
```

An image is a link with a `!` in front; the text in brackets becomes the
caption. In a table, the `|` characters don't need to line up, but it's easier
to read when they do. RStudio's **Visual** editor (the button at the top left
of the editor) lets you edit Markdown as formatted text and insert tables,
images, and links from menus, and switch back to **Source** to see the
Markdown.

::: {.tip}
**Literal characters.** To show a character that Markdown would otherwise
interpret, like `*` or `#`, put a backslash in front: `\*not italic\*`.
:::

### Learning more {-}

- [CommonMark's 10-minute tutorial](https://commonmark.org/help/tutorial/):
  short interactive lessons, typed in your browser. Start here.
- [Markdown Tutorial](https://www.markdowntutorial.com/): more interactive
  lessons.
- [The Markdown Guide](https://www.markdownguide.org/): clear reference, with
  a [one-page cheat sheet](https://www.markdownguide.org/cheat-sheet/).
- [GitHub's guide to writing
  Markdown](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/writing-on-github/getting-started-with-writing-and-formatting-on-github/basic-writing-and-formatting-syntax),
  for README files on GitHub.
- For R Markdown: RStudio's [introductory
  tutorial](https://rmarkdown.rstudio.com/lesson-1.html), the [R Markdown
  cheat sheet](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/rmarkdown.pdf), and the
  free books [*R Markdown: The Definitive
  Guide*](https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown/) and [*R Markdown
  Cookbook*](https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown-cookbook/).
- RStudio's [Visual
  editor](https://rstudio.github.io/visual-markdown-editing/) documentation.

::: {.exercise #ex-project}
Set up a project of your own: your thesis project, a side project, or this
class.

1. Make the project directory with `data`, `scripts`, `results`, `figs`,
   and `manuscript` folders, and a subdirectory in `data/` for each of your
   data sets, using a single `mkdir` command with brace expansion. Check the
   result with `find . -type d`.
2. Make it an RStudio project.
3. Download some data into `data/`. If you don't have any yet, download the
   *P. tricornutum* annotation (the `_genomic.gff.gz` file in the same NCBI
   directory as the genome; Section \@ref(download) shows how). Verify it
   with `md5sum` (Section \@ref(checksums)), and write a
   `data/README.md` that describes it.
4. Create `notebook.Rmd`. Make a dated entry recording the commands you used
   in step 3, and a software table with the version of `curl` you used. End the
   notebook with a `sessionInfo()` chunk. Knit it.
5. Write a top-level `README.md` that describes the project in a few
   sentences, with a heading, a bulleted list of the folders, a link, and a
   species name in italics.
6. In `results/`, make three run directories with different parameter
   settings in their names, each holding a small output file (`echo` some text
   into it). Make a `FINAL_PUBLISHED_RESULT` link to one of the files, and
   check it with `ls -l` and `head`. Then make a broken link on purpose, from
   the top of the project, and see what `ls -l` and `head` do with it.
:::

::: {.exercise}
Work through CommonMark's [10-minute Markdown
tutorial](https://commonmark.org/help/tutorial/). Then add a table and an
image to your notebook, and knit it again.
:::

## Summary {#project-summary}

| Item                  | What it's for                                               |
|-----------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|
| `data/`               | raw data, read-only, with a `README.md` describing sources  |
| `scripts/`            | code                                                        |
| `results/`            | intermediate files made by scripts                          |
| `figs/`               | figures made by scripts                                     |
| `manuscript/`         | writing                                                     |
| subdirectories        | where they help: `data/` by source, `results/` by dated analysis run |
| `README.md`           | what the project is                                         |
| `notebook.Rmd`        | dated record of everything you did, with commands, versions, and results |
| `project.Rproj`       | makes the directory an RStudio project                      |
| `mkdir -p dir/{a,b}/{c,d}` | make a whole tree of directories at once               |
| `ln -s run/file FINAL_PUBLISHED_RESULT` | mark the exact output used in a publication |
